narrative:
The model determined that you have an 88.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest influences. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 also worked against you, though its effect was smaller; it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and added a modest additional push toward a failing outcome.

Your LSAT score of 29, middle-family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race played little or no role in the final prediction. The system focused almost entirely on your school performance signals.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking the LSAT and aiming for a substantially higher score, or strengthening your academic record through additional coursework that demonstrates mastery at a higher level. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current profile. (198 words)
